questions.q: A patient with long-standing diabetes reports early satiety and vomiting of undigested food several hours after meals. Which physiological abnormality most directly explains this pattern?
options: Accelerated gastric emptying due to excessive vagal activity
Delayed gastric emptying due to impaired autonomic regulation of gastric motility
Failure of the ileocaecal sphincter to relax
Excessive segmentation in the colon
questions.explain: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can impair vagal and enteric control of gastric motor function, producing gastroparesis. Delayed gastric emptying causes early satiety, postprandial fullness and vomiting of retained food.

questions.q: A meal enters the small intestine and stimulates local mixing contractions that repeatedly divide and recombine the intestinal contents. What is the principal function of this movement?
options: Rapid propulsion of contents into the rectum
Mixing chyme with digestive secretions and bringing it into contact with the mucosa
Preventing all movement during digestion
Moving bile from the gallbladder into the duodenum
questions.explain: Segmentation consists of localised rhythmic contractions of circular smooth muscle. It mixes chyme with digestive secretions and repeatedly exposes it to the absorptive surface; peristalsis is the principal propulsive pattern.

questions.q: A drug selectively suppresses activity in the myenteric plexus while leaving the submucosal plexus relatively intact. Which change is most likely?
options: Reduced intestinal motility and propulsion
Complete loss of mucosal blood flow
Increased gastric acid secretion
Failure of pancreatic enzyme synthesis
questions.explain: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is principally concerned with gastrointestinal motility, including tone, peristalsis and propagation of contractions. The submucosal (Meissner) plexus has a stronger role in local secretion and blood-flow regulation.

open.q: State the principal function of the myenteric plexus and contrast it with that of the submucosal plexus.
accept: Myenteric plexus regulates motility; submucosal plexus regulates secretion and local blood flow
Auerbach controls motility; Meissner controls secretion

questions.q: A local intestinal reflex increases epithelial secretion after stimulation of the mucosa. Which enteric plexus is most directly associated with this response?
options: Myenteric plexus
Submucosal plexus
Celiac ganglion
Pelvic splanchnic ganglion
questions.explain: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies in the submucosa and regulates mucosal secretion, absorption-related activity and local blood flow. The myenteric plexus is more closely associated with gastrointestinal motility.

open.q: Which enteric plexus is most directly involved in regulating intestinal mucosal secretion?
accept: Submucosal plexus
Meissner plexus

questions.q: Acidic chyme enters the duodenum and stimulates a hormone that increases pancreatic bicarbonate-rich fluid secretion. Which cell type releases this hormone?
options: G cells of the gastric antrum
S cells of the duodenal mucosa
I cells of the jejunum
K cells of the proximal small intestine
questions.explain: Acid in the duodenal lumen stimulates S cells to release secretin. Secretin acts principally on pancreatic ductal cells to increase bicarbonate-rich fluid secretion, helping neutralise gastric acid.

open.q: Name the hormone released by duodenal S cells in response to acid and state its principal pancreatic effect.
accept: Secretin; increases bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid secretion
Secretin stimulates pancreatic ductal HCO3 secretion

questions.q: Fatty acids and amino acid products enter the duodenum after a meal. Which response is most characteristic of cholecystokinin?
options: Gallbladder contraction and increased pancreatic enzyme secretion
Increased gastric emptying and reduced pancreatic secretion
Increased gastric acid secretion with relaxation of the gallbladder
Suppression of pancreatic enzyme secretion
questions.explain: Cholecystokinin (CCK), released mainly by I cells in the proximal small intestine in response to fats and protein digestion products, contracts the gallbladder and stimulates pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion. It also slows gastric emptying and potentiates secretin's pancreatic action.

open.q: Give two major digestive actions of cholecystokinin (CCK).
accept: Contracts gallbladder and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion
Stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion; contracts gallbladder

questions.q: A nutrient-containing meal stimulates K cells in the proximal small intestine. Which hormone is released and what is one of its important actions?
options: Gastrin; stimulates gastric acid secretion
GIP; enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion
Secretin; stimulates gallbladder contraction
CCK; inhibits pancreatic enzyme secretion
questions.explain: Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP), also called glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, is released from K cells in the proximal small intestine in response to oral nutrients, especially glucose and fat. It enhances insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner and can inhibit gastric activity.

open.q: Which hormone is released from intestinal K cells after oral nutrient intake, and what is its incretin action?
accept: GIP; increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion
Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide enhances insulin release

questions.q: A patient has marked gastric acid secretion after a protein-rich meal. Which mechanism normally helps limit further gastrin release as the antral contents become highly acidic?
options: Low antral pH suppresses gastrin release, partly through somatostatin
Low antral pH stimulates G cells to release more gastrin
Secretin directly stimulates G cells
Acid activates the myenteric plexus to release gastrin
questions.explain: Gastrin release is stimulated by peptides, gastric distension and vagal input, but strongly acidic antral contents inhibit G-cell activity. Somatostatin from antral D cells contributes to this negative-feedback control.

open.q: How does a very low antral pH regulate gastrin secretion?
accept: It inhibits gastrin release, with somatostatin contributing to the inhibition
Low pH suppresses G cells via somatostatin

questions.q: During an intestinal inhibitory reflex, enteric neurons release a mediator that relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle and contributes to sphincter relaxation. Which mediator is most likely?
options: Gastrin
Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)
Secretin
GIP
questions.explain: VIP is an inhibitory enteric neurotransmitter that promotes smooth-muscle relaxation and can stimulate intestinal secretion. It participates in relaxation responses, including receptive relaxation and sphincter relaxation.

open.q: Name an inhibitory enteric neurotransmitter that relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle.
accept: Vasoactive intestinal peptide
VIP

questions.q: A patient receives an oral glucose load. Compared with an equivalent intravenous glucose load, the oral load produces a greater insulin response. Which gastrointestinal signal helps explain this difference?
options: Gastrin released from antral G cells
GIP released from intestinal K cells
Secretin released from duodenal S cells
Motilin released during fasting
questions.explain: The incretin effect is partly mediated by GIP from intestinal K cells (and GLP-1 from L cells). These hormones enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion after oral nutrient exposure, so oral glucose evokes a greater insulin response than intravenous glucose at a matched glycaemia.

open.q: Which intestinal incretin hormone is released from K cells and contributes to the greater insulin response after oral glucose?
accept: GIP
Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide

questions.q: During the pharyngeal phase of swallowing, which event protects the lower respiratory tract from aspiration?
options: Closure of the laryngeal inlet with vocal-fold adduction and elevation of the larynx
Relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter throughout the entire phase
Opening of the glottis with deep inspiration
Voluntary contraction of the diaphragm
questions.explain: The pharyngeal phase is involuntary and includes elevation of the soft palate, laryngeal elevation and closure of the laryngeal inlet, vocal-fold adduction and a brief deglutition apnoea. These coordinated events protect the airway while the bolus passes.

open.q: During the pharyngeal phase of swallowing, which event protects the lower respiratory tract from aspiration?
accept: Closure of the laryngeal inlet with vocal-fold adduction and laryngeal elevation

questions.q: A patient has impaired relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter during swallowing. Which muscle normally forms the principal functional component of this sphincter?
options: Cricopharyngeus
Inferior pharyngeal constrictor only
Thyropharyngeus
Upper third of the oesophageal circular muscle
questions.explain: The cricopharyngeus, part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor, forms the principal muscular component of the upper oesophageal sphincter. It relaxes during the pharyngeal phase to permit bolus entry into the oesophagus.

open.q: A patient has impaired relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter during swallowing. Which muscle normally forms the principal functional component of this sphincter?
accept: Cricopharyngeus

questions.q: During normal swallowing, the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes before the peristaltic wave reaches the gastro-oesophageal junction. What is this response called?
options: Receptive relaxation
Gastric accommodation
Segmentation
Migrating motor complex
questions.explain: The lower oesophageal sphincter undergoes deglutitive relaxation, coordinated with the swallowing reflex, before the peristaltic wave arrives. This permits passage of the bolus into the stomach; vagal pathways and inhibitory enteric neurons are involved.

open.q: During normal swallowing, the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes before the peristaltic wave reaches the gastro-oesophageal junction. What is this response called?
accept: Deglutitive relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter

questions.q: Which is the principal physiological advantage of mastication before swallowing?
options: It increases the surface area of food and mixes it with saliva
It converts all dietary starch directly to glucose
It initiates gastric acid secretion through direct stimulation of parietal cells
It prevents all microbial entry into the alimentary canal
questions.explain: Mastication reduces particle size, increasing the surface area available to digestive enzymes, and mixes food with saliva to form a lubricated bolus. It has both voluntary and reflex components.

open.q: Which is the principal physiological advantage of mastication before swallowing?
accept: Increases food surface area and mixes food with saliva

questions.q: Which statement best describes the neural control of salivary secretion?
options: Both parasympathetic and sympathetic stimulation can increase secretion, with parasympathetic stimulation producing copious watery saliva
Salivary secretion is controlled primarily by circulating gastrin
Only sympathetic stimulation can initiate salivation
Salivary glands secrete at a constant rate independent of neural activity
questions.explain: Salivary secretion is predominantly under autonomic neural control. Parasympathetic stimulation produces abundant watery secretion, while sympathetic stimulation can also increase secretion, often with a smaller, more protein-rich component.

open.q: Which statement best describes the neural control of salivary secretion?
accept: Both autonomic divisions stimulate salivary secretion; parasympathetic stimulation produces copious watery saliva

questions.q: As salivary flow rate increases, how does the ionic composition of final saliva generally change?
options: It becomes less hypotonic because ductal modification has less time to occur
It becomes increasingly hypertonic because ducts actively add sodium
Its sodium and chloride concentrations fall to zero
Its composition remains identical to plasma at all flow rates
questions.explain: Primary acinar saliva is approximately isotonic. Ducts reabsorb sodium and chloride and secrete potassium and bicarbonate while being relatively impermeable to water. At high flow rates, there is less time for modification, so final saliva becomes less hypotonic and sodium and chloride concentrations rise.

open.q: As salivary flow rate increases, how does the ionic composition of final saliva generally change?
accept: It becomes less hypotonic as sodium and chloride concentrations rise

questions.q: A patient with severe xerostomia has difficulty forming a food bolus. Which salivary component is especially important for lubrication?
options: Mucin
Pepsin
Intrinsic factor
Bile salts
questions.explain: Salivary mucins are glycoproteins that lubricate the oral cavity and help bind food particles into a cohesive bolus for swallowing. Saliva also contains bicarbonate, electrolytes, amylase and antimicrobial factors.

open.q: A patient with severe xerostomia has difficulty forming a food bolus. Which salivary component is especially important for lubrication?
accept: Mucin

questions.q: Which statement best describes segmentation contractions in the small intestine?
options: They are rhythmic local mixing contractions that expose chyme to the mucosal surface
They are the principal mechanism for rapid long-distance propulsion of faeces
They occur only when extrinsic sympathetic nerves are activated
They are generated exclusively by the longitudinal muscle layer
questions.explain: Segmentation consists of rhythmic contractions, predominantly involving circular smooth muscle, that divide and remix intestinal contents. This promotes contact between chyme and the absorptive mucosa; peristalsis is more directly responsible for propulsion.

open.q: Which statement best describes segmentation contractions in the small intestine?
accept: Rhythmic local mixing contractions that increase mucosal contact

questions.q: A patient develops steatorrhoea after a disorder that reduces delivery of bile to the duodenum. Which action of cholecystokinin normally helps coordinate bile delivery after a fatty meal?
options: Contraction of the gallbladder with relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi
Relaxation of the gallbladder with contraction of the sphincter of Oddi
Inhibition of pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion
Stimulation of gastric emptying
questions.explain: CCK is released from intestinal I cells in response to fat and protein digestion products. It contracts the gallbladder and promotes sphincter of Oddi relaxation, facilitating bile entry into the duodenum.

open.q: How does CCK promote delivery of bile into the duodenum?
accept: Contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi

questions.q: A meal rich in fat remains in the stomach longer than a comparable carbohydrate meal. Which intestinal signal contributes most directly to this slowing of gastric emptying?
options: Cholecystokinin released in response to fat in the duodenum
Motilin released during fasting
Gastrin released by gastric distension
Salivary amylase entering the stomach
questions.explain: Fat in the duodenum stimulates CCK release. CCK slows gastric emptying and coordinates delivery of nutrients with the digestive capacity of the small intestine.

open.q: Which intestinal hormone slows gastric emptying in response to fat entering the duodenum?
accept: Cholecystokinin
CCK
